title: How to Face a Hard Diagnosis
excerpt: The day the news comes, the floor drops out. You cannot control the disease. You can decide, slowly, how you will walk through what it asks of you.
body:
There is a before and an after, and the line between them is a sentence said in a quiet room by someone in a white coat. Before, you were a person with plans. After, you are a patient with a prognosis. The diagnosis does not just threaten your body. It rewrites your future, shrinks your horizon, and hands you a fear that wakes you at three in the morning. If you have just crossed that line, I am not going to tell you it will be fine, because I do not know that, and you would not believe me. I am going to tell you how people of faith have walked through this valley without pretending it is not a valley.

## Let yourself be afraid

The first thing the brave Christians around you may imply is that fear is a failure, that if you really trusted God you would not be afraid. That is a lie, and it adds shame to suffering. Jesus, in the garden, was "sorrowful and troubled" and asked for the cup to pass. Fear in the face of death is not weak faith. It is the honest response of a creature who loves being alive. Do not pile guilt on top of the diagnosis. Feel the fear, and bring it where Jesus brought his, to the Father, on your face, in the dark.

## Separate the facts from the catastrophe

In the first days the mind runs ahead to every worst case at once, dying a hundred deaths before any of them arrives. Bring it back. Get the actual facts: the diagnosis, the options, the questions you still need answered. Write them down, because you will not remember what the doctor said. Bring someone with you to appointments to be your second set of ears. Fear feeds on the unknown, and replacing the imagined catastrophe with the real facts, hard as they are, is itself a mercy. Fight the disease you have, not the ten you have invented.

## Take it one day at a time, literally

Jesus said not to be anxious about tomorrow, that today has enough trouble of its own, and a hard diagnosis is where that sentence stops being a platitude and becomes a survival strategy. You cannot live the whole illness today. You can only live today. Some days you can only live the next hour. Shorten the horizon to what you can actually carry. The manna in the wilderness came one day at a time and could not be stored, and that was not God being stingy. It was God teaching a frightened people to trust him for today and let tomorrow come when it comes.

## Let people in

The instinct is to protect everyone, to carry it alone, to not be a burden. Refuse that instinct. You were not built to bear this by yourself, and the people who love you would rather carry it with you than be kept outside the door. Tell your church. Let them bring meals and drive you to treatment and pray over you. Receiving help is not weakness. It is the body of Christ doing what it exists to do, and depriving them of the chance to love you is a kind of pride dressed as consideration.

## Hold your life and your hope at the same time

Faith does not ask you to stop fighting for your life. Treat the disease, take the medicine, do everything within reach. And underneath the fight, hold the deeper hope, the one that does not depend on the scan results. The Christian does not face death as someone with nothing on the far side of it. The empty tomb means the worst thing is not the last thing. You can fight to live with everything you have and still know that if the fight is lost, you are not.

**This week:** Write down the three questions that are frightening you most about your diagnosis. Bring them to your next appointment and ask them out loud, or call the nurse line if you cannot wait. Then read 2 Corinthians 4:16 through 18, where Paul names the wasting-away body and the unseen weight of glory in the same breath, and let both be true.

A hard diagnosis takes much from you, but it does not get to take everything, and the things it cannot reach are the ones that matter most. It cannot reach the love around you. It cannot reach the God who has already gone through death ahead of you and come out the other side. You did not choose this valley. You do get to choose, one day at a time, that you will not walk it alone or without hope.
